newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Peters' key priorities.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Peters' key priorities.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Oct 30 - The Beehive has been reduced to a mausoleum, with some living corpses wandering around, according to one government official.
But this week NZ First leader Winston Peters is due to pick up the pace in coalition talks.

He has to make the leap from being the chief practitioner of the politics of grievance to being an actively constructive architect of government policy. The question is whether he is, essentially, a closet socialist, or a tough-love fiscally-responsible free-marketeer.
On the evidence of his anti-Asian, anti-foreign investment stance pre-election, the assumption has been that he leans towards Muldoonist-style interventionism.
But when negotiations on coalition with Labour or National begin in earnest, the first indications may emerge on the priorities Peters attaches to specific policies.

If NZ First puts at the top of its agenda its community work and universal student allowance programmes, then it will be a clear signal that Peters is reflecting the philosophy that lay behind his Ka Awatea programme when he was briefly minister of Maori affairs in the Bolger government.

In that programme, Peters wanted to build a foundation on which Maori could break away from a debilitating dependency culture. In putting the focus on combating poverty and unemployment, NZ First would not necessarily be guaranteeing jobs for everyone, but would be aiming to provide everyone with purposeful activity, either through community work or study.
The conventional wisdom has been that workfare schemes require a demeaning intrusion by bureaucrats into people's private lives to assess their entitlement to benefit.
But Peters has shown no respect for conventional wisdom. And there is clear enough evidence that institutions like Social Welfare need to undertake a rigorous self-examination.

Reconstruction of the welfare state to serve people, particularly Maori, more effectively is a goal that would enable him to reclaim the decent society, which National campaigned for in 1990 - and which the Bolger government, in Peters' subsequent claim, betrayed with its Mother Of All Budgets.

If on the surface, NZ First in this respect has more in common with Labour than National, the advantage lies with National in that a coalition between it and NZ First would have the numbers to carry through the main policy planks NZ First wants to implement.
NZ First with Labour could only succeed providing it has support from the Alliance -- and thus the credit for any positive achievement might slip from the grasp of NZ First.

Peters has a vested interest in marginalising the Labour Party. NZ First wins its support from angry young Maori and angry Pakeha pensioners. Both these groups have moved across from Labour. By forming a coalition with Labour, Peters would be telling his brown and grey supporters that there is no real difference in voting for either NZ First or Labour.

Those who have been close to the talks -- and knew Peters when he was previously a cabinet minister -- say that he has matured as a politician. This is evident, they insist, from the tight discipline Peters has enforced on his colleagues.

NZ First is conscious it may have only one chance to roll the dice. If it is to tie down a long-term future in the New Zealand political spectrum, it has to deliver tangible results to its supporters.

At the same time, the fiscal constraints limit the room for manoeuvre. Briefings by Treasury and the Reserve Bank to political parties, according to Act NZ finance spokesman Rodney Hide, have indicated that the economy is on a knife edge.

The fiscal position has slipped considerably, with the consequence that interest rates are very high and the exchange rae is punishingly high. Spending for 1997/98 is already $1.8 billion up from what was planned just a year ago.
So this week Peters will have to focus on just how he can implement what he sees as priority commitments by NZ First -- and whether Labour or National will accept those comitments.
Note - The views expressed are those of the author and are not attributable to Reuters.
